questions.question: Describe the housing of working-class families in industrial towns in the 1840s and explain why it was so poor.
questions.expected_answer: Many families lived in back-to-back houses sharing back and side walls, with windows on one side only, no yard or through draught, often one room up and one down, built around narrow enclosed courts. The poorest lived in damp, dark cellars that flooded, or in lodging houses. Large families shared one or two rooms and took in lodgers. It was poor because towns grew very fast as people arrived from the countryside and Ireland, workers needed to live near the mills, there were no building regulations or planning, and builders and landlords built cheaply and densely to maximise rents.

questions.question: Explain how lack of clean water and sanitation led to disease, naming three diseases, and describe the findings and significance of the Chadwick report of 1842 and John Snow's work of 1854.
questions.expected_answer: Few houses had piped water; families used shared pumps drawing on polluted rivers. One privy over a cesspool served many households and overflowed into yards and wells, and streets were undrained. Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated water, typhus through lice in overcrowded housing, and tuberculosis through the air in damp crowded rooms. Chadwick showed that disease was linked to dirt, poor drainage and bad water and that the poor died far younger, with an average age at death of 17 for Manchester labourers against 38 for professionals, leading to the 1848 Public Health Act. Snow mapped cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump and showed that cholera spread through water, not bad air, which later helped justify sewers and clean water.

questions.question: Explain the 1834 Poor Law and the principle of less eligibility, describe conditions in a workhouse, and explain why the workhouse was so feared.
questions.expected_answer: The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act grouped parishes into unions that built workhouses; able-bodied people seeking relief were, in principle, to receive it only inside. Less eligibility meant conditions inside had to be worse than those of the poorest independent labourer, so only the desperate would apply. Inmates wore uniforms, families were separated, food was plain, work was hard and dull, such as stone breaking, bone crushing and oakum picking, and rules were strict; the Andover scandal of 1845 exposed starving inmates. It was feared because it meant losing family life, freedom and respectability, and it carried deep shame.
